newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian miners watch for Busang repercussions.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian miners watch for Busang repercussions.

text.p: Indonesia's mining community is watching for possible repercussions from the Busang gold scandal as local and Canadian police investigate the biggest mining fraud in history, industry sources said at the weekend.
The government is expected to demand foreign mining firms allocate it a 10-percent stake in future projects as part of a tightening of mining rules in the aftermath of Busang.

Although the sources hailed U.S. Newmont Gold Corp's thwarting of a government attempt to secure a stake in its Batu Hijau copper and gold project, they expect similar moves could be made in new projects involving foreign companies.
Newmont came into spotlight last week when Mines and Energy Minister Ida Bagus Sudjana said the government was seeking a stake in the project, citing "nationalistic interests".
Newmont rejected the bid, saying it was not economically feasible as it already had a local partner in the $1.9 billion project that is set to begin production in 1999.
"I am glad the government and Newmont have been able to resolve the Batu Hijau issue," Beni Wahju, secretary general of the Indonesian Mining Association told Reuters.
"Minister Sudjana should be commended for accepting Newmont's decision...and the resolution of the issue will reinforce confidence in the Indonesian mining sector."
The Batu Hijau property contains an estimated 12.1 million ounces of gold and 10.6 billion pounds of copper.
The government exerts control over mining companies through contracts of work, which carry with them vital state approval needed to explore for and mine minerals in Indonesia.
Industry officials said some 160 foreign companies and their local partners had applied for contracts.
"It is going to be very interesting to see whether the government will insert the condition into the seventh generation contracts of work," one industry official said.
"It can do so even though the contracts have been approved in principle...but it would be bad practice because negotiations over the contracts have been concluded," he said.
"Nearly half the companies involved are junior exploration companies, which are going to find it difficult to raise funds because of Busang," one industry official said.

The fabled Busang gold discovery collapsed last week after an independent audit revealed the property -- touted by Canadian exploration firm Bre-X Minerals Ltd as the biggest gold find this century -- contained no viable gold deposit.
Consultant Strathcona Mineral Services Ltd said data on Busang in Indonesian Borneo were falsified on an unprecedented scale.
Bre-X sought court protection from its creditors on Thursday, the day after the company was delisted from the Toronto Stock Exchange where it was once courted feverishly by investors.

Canadian and Indonesian police have opened investigations into the scandal, with a senior officer from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police holding talks with local police on Friday to possibly lay the groundwork for joint action.

Brigadier-General Ahwil Luthan, secretary of the National Central Bureau, which handles investigations requiring Interpol assistance, said his department had begun gathering evidence of possible commercial crime in the Busang debacle.

"We are waiting to see what the extent of the Busang fallout will be," one industry official said. "Whether it will involve action against government officials or stop with the tightening of mining regulations, we will have to wait and see."
